<reason>A wins the proportionality clash. B established a credible, ultimately conceded mechanism: aging legal suppliers make teenage access harder. But A explained why that benefit does not automatically justify lifelong exclusion of already-dependent adults and expanded enforcement against adult proxy purchases. B’s answers—attrition, administrative simplicity, and cessation support—did not adequately resolve those burdens. A answered the pressure without demanding perfect enforcement, while B repeatedly overstated the connection between legal eligibility and inevitable recruitment. A’s closing also correctly defended adult consequences as central to judging a lifelong policy.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A exposed the weakness in B’s grandfathering rationale: the cutoff preserves older nonsmokers’ access while excluding younger dependent smokers. B explained why birthdates are administratively convenient, but did not convincingly justify treating equivalent dependence differently. This made A’s fairness objection concrete rather than merely formal.</best_rebuttal>
